Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment: There was a PHMSA workshop in 2016 done because of the need for revision of the regulations for LNG facilities.  PHMSA-2022-0076-0013_attachment_1.pdf talks about the workshop and how it led to work for Sandia Corporation to perform because of a need for calculations regarding overpressures that could occur during zero-wind conditions at export terminals.  Those calculations should have been done by now and made public but I cannot find them.  Also there is discussion of a facility built for direct testing of behavior of LNG under various conditions, the LGFSTF facility.  Surely that facility could quickly do experiments to confirm or deny claims made by a computer model that has not been subjected to peer review and is being kept secret even though it apparently has never been run under zero-wind conditions which are common in our Southwest Louisiana LNG terminal locations.

Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment: There is indeed a need for revision of the LNG regulations. That is something that has been called for repeatedly by people from different perspectives. There is even a  PHMSA website with some grave concerns and recommendations expressed by a leading world-recognized expert in the field, Dr. Jerry Havens.    He has been asking for revisions since a 2016 PHMSA workshop that PHMSA arranged in anticipation of the needed revisions.  That link to 15 documents that cannot be ignored during this new effort, is: www.regulations.gov/search?filter=PHMSA-2022-0076.   If you were not to address those existing petitions and their reasonings in this process it would nullify, legally, whatever your eventual moves might be in addressing the need for updated and pertinent regulations.     The issues Dr. Havens raises involve the reality that NFPA59A attempts to provide adequate fire safety protection for people but is hamstrung by the problems of inadequate computer modeling, done without model evaluation nor peer review, and still kept secret.  As for DOT expecting Americans to be able to provide fully-informed comments when much of the Federal Register notice requires knowledge of the contents of  NFPA59A, for a citizen to read that document he would have to pay NFPA $157 dollars.  Do you really think that the thousands of people in a neighborhood adjacent to an LNG terminal each have an extra $157 dollars to spend to make sure that their worries are properly-addressed?   I bought a copy several years ago but given the new and inflated cost I cannot do that year-in-and-year out.  Besides, what I read in my copy years ago did not address the key problems I see here in the Southwest Louisiana LNG "Buildout Zone" where we now have 3 operational facilities with 6 more planned.  PLEASE DO revise the rules, but do it honestly, transparently, and with "Safety First" which has always been the American way.  Thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments.

Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment: See attached file.   The Office of Inspector General published a good report that should not be forgotten as you revise the LNG regulations. It is dated April 28, 2020, is Report No. ST2020031, and is entitled "PHMSA Has Incomplete Guidance for Evaluating the Siting of Proposed Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities and Monitoring State Pipeline Safety Programs."  The consequences of that have become clear with the placement of Lake Charles LNG, Louisiana LNG, Magnolia LNG, Cameron LNG, Venture Global LNG, Venture Global CP2 LNG, Commonwealth LNG, and Cheniere Sabine Pass LNG, all in Southwest Louisiana.

Title: Comment from RESTORE

Title: Comment from RESTORE

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment: The exclusion of ‘‘any part of a structure or equipment located in navigable waters’’ should be revoked.  Equipment in navigable waters are required to be externally protected by a cathodic protection system.  Such systems, even if properly operated, can cause hydrogen embrittlement of susceptible materials which can lead to cracking and potentially catastrophic failure.  The base material and welds need to be evaluated if there is not a history of use in such service.

Title: Comment from Kristin Johnson
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Susan  Allmeroth
Comment:
Public Comment on Docket No. PHMSA-2019-0091: Opposing Expansion and Weakening of LNG Facility Regulations

I write in unequivocal opposition to any regulatory changes that would weaken oversight of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) facilities or facilitate their expansion under the guise of “modernization.” Any move to relax safety, environmental, or community protections in LNG infrastructure is not only irresponsible—it is a direct threat to our climate, to public safety, and to the rights of Indigenous peoples and frontline communities.

LNG infrastructure is a fossil fuel system—period. It extends the lifespan of a dying industry at the expense of a livable future. It locks in decades of methane leakage, ecological disruption, and carbon emissions, even as the science is screaming that we have no time left. PHMSA must not be complicit in a regulatory rollback that endangers lives and undercuts national and international climate commitments.

I point specifically to the precedent set by the exclusion of the Alaska Region from the 10th National OCS Oil and Gas Leasing Program. Despite vast theoretical resource estimates—29.88 billion barrels of oil equivalent in the Chukchi Sea and 8.61 in the Beaufort Sea—current leasing has yielded nearly no production. As of April 1, 2025, only three leases in the Beaufort Sea produce anything; none of the eight active leases in Cook Inlet are producing at all. This is not a strategic asset. It is a stranded liability.

Any attempt to justify LNG expansion in light of this record defies reason.

Furthermore, I stand with the Sila Inuat and the Grandmothers of Goodness, who are defending Arctic homelands and global climate stability against extractive violence. Their leadership should guide federal decision-making—not industry lobbyists who profit from regulatory erosion.

PHMSA must:

• Halt any proposal that eases siting, permitting, or operational requirements for LNG facilities.

• Require a full lifecycle climate and community impact analysis under NEPA for every LNG-related rule or project.

• Acknowledge the historical and ongoing harm LNG infrastructure poses to Indigenous sovereignty, health, and culture.

• Reject any framing that casts LNG as a “bridge fuel.” That bridge leads to climate catastrophe.

There is no safe way to expand LNG. There is no just path through fossil fuels.

PHMSA must stop insulating this industry from accountability. You are not just regulating pipelines. You are deciding whether people live or die, whether homes are swallowed by sea or protected, whether our children inherit resilience or ruin.

Say no to LNG expansion. Say yes to survival.

PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about PHMSA’s upcoming update of LNG safety regulations. 

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. Ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions.. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Director Duffy,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Mark Jackson
Comment:
Dear Director Duffy,
 I'm so glad that the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) has announced an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking to change LNG safety regulations. The US has become the world's top exporter of LNG, and yet the current safeguards are inadequate in protecting workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure, and require updates to be effective. 

Please include the following in the new LNG Safety Regulations. First, there has to be more transparency when it comes to safety management plans, risk mitigation, emergency evacuation routes, and other issues that directly relate to the safety of the surrounding communities. While there are legitimate issues regarding the security of LNG export terminals, there are ways for PHMSA to ensure the community has access to information and a voice in safety management. In addition, PHMSA must make a version of its inspection reports available to the public, especially if there are code violations that put the community at risk. Second, PHMSA must enact a “reverse 911” system to alert impacted communities when there are leaks and explosions. Messages should provide residents with instructions on whether to evacuate or shelter in place, or to take other actions as needed. Third, workers at LNG export terminals and associated infrastructure are often the first to know about problems, and can know about issues long before they manifest into leaks, vapor clouds, or explosions. Reporting issues, however, can be challenging and put workers at risk of retribution, including losing their job. PHMSA must create an anonymous reporting hotline so that workers can anonymously and securely report issues that can be followed up with an inspection. 
Thank you for working to protect our health and safety!

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Mark Wyzenbeek
85345
markwyz@yahoo.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Anna Stusser

(360) 888-6932

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Anne Tuddenham
94530
hatuddenham@gmail.com

Title: Comment from Linda K Sturdevant
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

 I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Jean Stephenson
84111
JLS1113@aol.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Judy Fairless
07059
8wildcat@optonline.net

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Ked Garden

kedz2garden@gmail.com
(619) 555-5555

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Felix Lee
98112
flee61255@gmail.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Gerald Kretmar
33331
kretmar@sbcglobal.net

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Linda Caputo
98005
lindacaputo@live.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Carla Hedden

(864) 638-7932

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Steven Hester
70058
hesters88@yahoo.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Jim P
95125
peckos@me.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Ishanee DeVas

(646) 479-8722

Title: Comment from Rhonda Carter
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
James Hamilton ''' Hamilton

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Michael O'Brien
53177
evilmob@msn.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Nancy Hayden
99224
gncrh@aol.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Blackie Strassburg
90245
moondrop7@gmail.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Susan Castelli-Hill
11747
joyoussafefree@yahoo.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Amy Anderson

amygreer@yahoo.com
(727) 555-1212

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Mary Doane
95076
murry@cruzio.com

Title: Comment from Sheri Kuticka
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

I am concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Carol Ng
90026
carolng38@yahoo.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Margrit Spear
91935
mbspear@sbcglobal.net

As an Amercian voter, I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a shocking number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Ruth Harmon
97086
tashamail@comcast.net

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Dania Smith
45203
dania@fuse.net

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Cesar Raposo
13760
1lusitano@outlook.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Dagmar Fabian
98225
dagmarfabian@gmail.com
(360) 366-8344

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
carol dickason
95476
dickason05@gmail.com

Title: Comment from Jesse Kirkham
Comment:
I am writing in response to the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) titled *“Pipeline Safety: Amendments to Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities”* to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen—not weaken—safety regulations for liquefied methane gas (LNG) export terminals.

The current safety standards, last updated in 2004, are dangerously outdated. Since then, the U.S. has become the world’s largest LNG exporter, with facilities operating at unprecedented scale and complexity. Yet the regulatory framework has not kept pace. Communities near these terminals have experienced explosions, leaks, and other serious incidents—clear evidence that stronger protections are urgently needed.

PHMSA’s own ANPRM acknowledges the need to modernize Part 193 of the pipeline safety regulations. However, we are deeply concerned by references to deregulatory executive orders and calls for cost-saving measures that prioritize industry profits over public safety. This is not the time to cut corners. It is the time to lead with science, transparency, and a commitment to protecting lives.

The agency must:
- **Update safety standards** to reflect modern LNG technologies and risks;
- **Require robust public engagement** and risk disclosure for communities near LNG terminals;
- **Ensure worker protections** through stronger training, emergency response, and oversight;
- **Reject any amendments** that would reduce safety requirements under the guise of efficiency.

PHMSA has a clear mandate: to protect people and the environment from the hazards of pipeline and LNG infrastructure. That mission cannot be fulfilled through deregulation. I urge you to center this rulemaking on public safety, not industry convenience.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Lisa Johnson
78240
lisa.j@satx.rr.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Ellen Evans
93422
elliepirelli57@gmail.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Dan O'Donnell
20008
danodonnell03@yahoo.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
C Harden
48892
chloe.a.harden@gmail.com

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Loretta Aja
08034
ajal@verizon.net

Title: Comment from Esther Juhl
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Edward Jazwinski

edlojaz2@cox.net
(702) 275-7776
