I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Jon Levin

backhoe-cabana-0b@icloud.com

Title: Comment from Nicole Berkheimer
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Dave Kashyap

(209) 225-5177

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Frank Thacker
45638
thackerdon1947@yahoo.com

My family and I are responding to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Anne Harvey
92130
aharvey@ucsd.edu

Title: Comment from Juanita Montano
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Kelly Thomas
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from MARGARET SOWERWINE
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

The existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 
Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, your process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. 

We must prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

To do so, seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. you should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, and how to avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution. 

The costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures should be the most important consideration when updating these guidelines. 

Thank you.

Title: Comment from Anita Youabian
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Lawrence Danner
53222
larsdan10@yahoo.com

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Title: Comment from Melania Padilla
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Dwayne Thomas

Title: Comment from Elizabeth Glaaser
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Bo Baggs
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Anita Youabian
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,

Title: Comment from Thomas Cole
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Lauren A.
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Jill Dahlman
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Heather Davis
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Gerda Brasser
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Lauri Moon
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Meeyah  Davis
Comment:
As a stakeholder, it is evident that updates to safety practices within PHMSA Part 193 LNG facility federal safety standards are urgently needed. However, in light of Executive Order 14154 and its successor directives aimed at reducing regulatory burdens, a new set of challenges has emerged for LNG oversight. This deregulatory pressure has not only constrained the agency’s ability to enforce comprehensive safety measures; it has also diluted the emphasis on proactive risk prevention (Executive Order 14154, 2025).

The dangers associated with LNG incidents are real. The Calcasieu Pass terminal in Louisiana, for example, reported multiple gas releases in early 2022; one event alone released approximately 180000 pounds of methane (EPA, 2022). Methane is a greenhouse gas that is over 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over 20 years; it poses serious safety and environmental risks (EPA, 2021). Such incidents underscore the persistent volatility of LNG infrastructure and the limitations of current standards in preventing or containing such releases. Robust safety standards, such as those initiated under the Obama-era Pipeline Safety, Integrity, and Compliance Act of 2011 and expanded in 2020, are essential; they include mandates for increased inspection intervals, integrity management programs, and incident reporting protocols (PHMSA, 2020). Yet enforcement remains inconsistent. A 2021 GAO report found that PHMSA struggled with inspector staffing shortages and delayed rulemaking; this weakened its capacity to hold operators accountable (GAO, 2021). How can we consider deregulation when current regulation is not maintained? While fulfilling these responsibilities may be difficult, that difficulty does not justify inaction; the potential costs include human lives, ecosystem damage, and local economic disruption. The 2004 Skikda LNG explosion in Algeria, which killed 27 people and caused over 900 million dollars in damage, serves as a reminder that worst-case scenarios are not hypothetical (U.S. Department of Energy, 2005). 

Although the deregulatory agenda promises economic growth, this potential must not outweigh tangible risks to public safety. Updating Part 193 is not just a technical necessity; it is a moral imperative. Yet, the objective of modernizing these standards is increasingly entangled with economic advantage, creating an apparent conflict of interest. The prevailing attitude suggests that safety improvements are acceptable only if they do not compromise profitability. This leads to a regulatory environment where meaningful reform is discouraged, not because it lacks scientific or operational merit but because it threatens to inconvenience productivity or profit margins. When financial priorities dictate the scope of safety regulation, the result is a system where protection is conditional; both the public and the workforce bear the consequences of regulatory compromise. The revision of Part 193 must not simply streamline compliance; it must recommit to safeguarding lives, land, and long-term sustainability.

Title: Comment from David Warner
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Anthony L. Barreiro
Comment:
Dear Director Duffy -- Liquefied natural gas safety regulations need to be improved to protect nearby communities and facility workers.  Current regulations are inadequate.  There have been too many explosions, leaks, and other unmitigated hazards at LNG facilities.  The Freeport Louisiana LNG explosion is only one example.  

Four changes are needed:  

Frontline communities need to have full and timely access to facility safety management plans, risk mitigation, emergency evacuation routes, and other issues that directly relate to the safety of the surrounding communities.  Facilities should not be able to hide behind specious assertions of trade secrets or security risks to keep from sharing basic safety information with people whose lives and property are in danger.  

Relevant information from PHMSA safety inspections must be shared with frontline communities, especially findings of unsafe conditions and code violations, so local authorities and citizens can take action to protect themselves and advocate for facilities to operate safely.  

PHMSA must enact a “reverse 911” system to alert impacted communities when there are leaks and explosions.  Messages should provide residents with instructions on whether to evacuate or shelter in place, or to take other actions as needed.  

LNG facility workers are the first to know of safety violations and unsafe conditions, but they are afraid to report them because they fear losing their jobs.  PHMSA needs to create an anonymous reporting hotline so that workers can anonymously and securely report issues that can be followed up with an inspection.  

America needs strong safety standards prioritizing community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export facilities.  

Thank you.

Title: Comment from Linda K Sturdevant
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment: The absence of any calculations, modeling, or field testing of the potential for explosive overpressures during zero-wind conditions at LNG facilities surrounded by storm surge walls (such as the existing Venture Global Calcasieu Pass, its proposed expansion CP2, and the permitted Commonwealth LNG, all in Cameron Parish just downstream from the existing Sempra Cameron LNG at Hackberry, LA) leaves unaddressed the possibility of a cascading catastrophe.  Zero wind conditions in this area happen almost every night during the hours before dawn.  Over a hundred households in Cameron and over 400 households in Hackberry could be incinerated without warning should the heavy hydrocarbon refrigerants at Venture Global leak, collect within the storm wall enclosure and then blast apart the massive LNG storage tanks and moored ships.  Should that happened after CP2 and Commonwealth are operational, not only would all the workers, residents, fishermen and shrimpers on their boats, any seamen on petrochemical supertankers or other cargo ships be burned, but that Calcasieu Ship Channel would be blocked indefinitely with debris rendering useless what the Port of Lake Charles calls “The Nation's Energy Corridor.”  If the massive amount of released liquefied natural gas remained unignited as it flowed in the narrow channel into Hackberry and sets off that LNG facility, the cascading disaster could be amplified reaching farther inland to the existing Trunkline (Lake Charles) LNG, the permitted Magnolia LNG, and the under-construction Driftwood (Woodside/Louisiana LNG) facilities putting into the flame zone many thousands of people.  If you are going to revise the LNG rules just this one situation makes it imperative that you do NOT de-regulate what is already a deficient control system. You must instead use this opportunity to fix its shortcomings and make it strong enough to keep people safe.    Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments. Michael Tritico, Biologist and President of RESTORE

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Theresa Corrigan
Comment:
I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Joanne Polayes
Comment:
I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Joanne Polayes

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Safety first, isn’t that a good rule?  I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Dear Director Duffy, 

I'm so glad that the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) has announced an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking to change LNG safety regulations. 

The need to get this right is urgent: the US has become the world's top exporter of LNG, and yet the current safeguards are inadequate in protecting workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure, and urgently require updates to be effective. 

We've seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. June 8 is the anniversary of the devastating Freeport LNG explosion – a disaster that made it clear the current protections are not working. 

That’s why I urge you to include the following in the new LNG Safety Regulations. First, there has to be more transparency when it comes to safety management plans, risk mitigation, emergency evacuation routes, and other issues that directly relate to the safety of the surrounding communities. As it is, LNG companies are able to hide information behind claims of trade secrets and national security. While there are legitimate issues regarding the security of LNG export terminals, there are ways for PHMSA to ensure the community has access to information and a voice in safety management. In addition, PHMSA must make a version of their inspection reports available to the public, especially if there are code violations that put the community at risk. Some parishes or counties are supposed to have local emergency planning committees, but these have failed to be an effective mechanism for communicating with the public or producing adequate emergency plans. 

Second, PHMSA must enact a “reverse 911” system to alert impacted communities when there are leaks and explosions. Messages should provide residents with instructions on whether to evacuate or shelter in place, or to take other actions as needed. 

Third, workers at LNG export terminals and associated infrastructure are often the first to know about problems, and can know about issues long before they manifest into leaks, vapor clouds, or explosions. Reporting issues, however, can be challenging and put workers at risk of retribution, including losing their job. PHMSA must create an anonymous reporting hotline so that workers can anonymously and securely report issues that can be followed up with an inspection. 

The government has an obligation to protect our communities by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. We need strong safety standards prioritizing community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure.

Thank you for working to protect our health and safety!

Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

Thank you for this opportunity.

I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM)  to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. 

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

Sincerely,
Tom Quinn
20015
tomquinn71@gmail.com

Title: Comment from Laurie Lagoe
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment:
During this Rules Revision one possible flaw in the regulations of LNG enterprises is the likelihood that safety risks involving the LNG tankers have not been fully-evaluated. 

 One such lapse is the failure of the Waterway Safety Assessments to anticipate the kind of concerns that have been expressed, just this week on the FERC website by an existing LNG export terminal at the mouth of the Calcasieu River. 

Another such lapse is FERC and the Coast Guard having allowed moored, loading LNG tankers to stick out over 100 feet from the Sempra Cameron export terminal into the narrow Ship Channel where passing oil, gasoline, jet fuel, LPG, and petrochemical tankers slide by frequently. 

 Another problem is that all of the LNG tankers are foreign-flagged which means that the Coast Guard is prohibited from full inspections, something quite important in the case of the Moss-Style tankers where the Coast Guard cannot even look under the weather covers to see if the insulation on the LNG cargo tanks is intact. That is an important problem given the insulation's thin aluminum skrim cover's vulnerability to damage which would allow the LNG in the tanks to warm up which could lead to the overwhelming of the ship's likely too few or undersized pressure relief valves which would result in a catastrophic fire. 

The details of that kind of situation have been presented to Admiral Arguin of the U.S. Coast Guard as well as to PHMSA. It will be impossible to hide this already known and recorded information should there be a catastrophic event, especially one in which a loading or transiting LNG tanker experiences a fire that spreads to a shore terminal which then terribly burns hundreds of neighbors.

 Rather than de-regulating LNG protocols it is past time to aggressively answer ALL of the fire safety questions honestly, transparently, and completely for the sake of ALL stakeholders.

Title: Comment from RESTORE
Comment:
07/06/2025  RESTORE's Final Comments on Proposed LNG Rules Revision 49 CFR part 193
 Docket Number PHMSA-2019-0091

Thank you for  giving the people a chance to comment on a bizarre proposal to de-regulate an enterprise that, for many different reasons, poses high risks of burning flesh.  RESTORE has submitted several separate sets of comments already but this one will try to list the key reasons that we see making any deregulation, instead of answering open questions, simply sheer malfeasance.

1. As has been carefully and completely explained Dr. Jerry Havens, PHD, in nearly two dozen postings on regulations.gov/search?filter=PHMSA-2022-0076, the risks associated with LNG export terminals may be seriously underestimated.
2. The models used in calculating those risks have not been run for zero-wind conditions – leaving unanswered the results of a situation in which the heavy hydrocarbon refrigerants could leak, spread across the facility forming a layer near the ground, and then ignite creating overpressures that could damage containments of LNG in storage tanks and piping that delivers the material to LNG tankers. That would produce a major cascading catastrophe that would put, not just the export terminal but the entire area into a blazing conflagration.
3. The primary model (FLACS) has been kept secret, has not even been subjected to peer review, so that makes questionable even the risk conclusions reached for the circumstances that were used during purported calculations and then presented to the public during the FERC EIS process.
4. The model's assumed concentrations of escaped refrigerants within the confining storm surge walls at Louisiana coastal LNG export terminals were not released making even less-credible the speculation that all risks would be kept onsite.
5. Maritime risks that could result in not just the loss of an LNG tankership and its crew but also nearby mariners on other ships, sportfishermen, commercial fishermen, shrimpers, crabbers, and oystermen, people whose homes and camps are along the ship channel, even an entire export terminal adjacent to a moored or transiting flaming LNG ship, have not been addressed. Those unaddressed risk issues include inadequate or out-of-date Waterway Suitability Assessments, LNG ships allowed to stick out into the pathway of other hazardous material carriers, the vulnerability of LNG cargo tank insulation on Moss-Style tankers along with the likelihood that their Pressure Relief Valve system is not able to handle cargo swelling should the insulation be damaged and fail, plus the rule against the U.S. Coast Guard being allowed to inspect under the weather covers of those ships (all foreign-flagged) to make sure the insulation is not damaged.
6. Experiences in the Calcasieu River ecosystem since the buildout of LNG terminals there have shown the FERC environmental assessments of no significant impact on aquatic organisms to have been wrong.  Instead of throwing away that process it must be fixed.
7. As the lead agency FERC may delegate to other Federal and State entities certain responsibilities, but ALL of those people exist for good reasons, reasons the public has entrusted them to understand.      
 
For the agencies that we, the people, created to serve as our protectors to cave in to political pressures originating with profiteering interests, with the result of de-regulation,  making more of us more and more vulnerable to horrible burns, is simply un-American.  Please don't aid and abet ignorance and greed.  Your good work is in the national interest.  An LNG disaster is not. 

Michael Tritico, Biologist and President of RESTORE
Restore Explicit Symmetry To Our Ravaged Earth
