Subject: Strengthen Oil and Gas Safety Standards -- Pipeline Safety: Amendments to Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities (Document ID: PHMSA-2019-0091-0012)

To Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy and Acting PHMSA Administrator Benjamin D. Kochman:

I'm so glad that the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) has announced an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking to change liquified methane gas (LNG) safety regulations. The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. However, I am deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that the PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety. I urge the PHMSA to strengthen safety rules for LNG export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

"It is horrifying that we have to fight our own government to save the environment."
-- Ansel Adams

The need to get this right is urgent: the US has become the world's top exporter of LNG, and yet the current safeguards are inadequate in protecting workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure, and urgently require updates to be effective. Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. June 8 was the third anniversary of the devastating 2022 Freeport LNG explosion—a disaster that made it clear the current protections are not working.

That’s why I urge you to include the following in the new LNG Safety Regulations:

First, there has to be more transparency when it comes to safety management plans, risk mitigation, emergency evacuation routes, and other issues that directly relate to the safety of the surrounding communities. As it is, LNG companies are able to hide information behind claims of trade secrets and national security. While there are legitimate issues regarding the security of LNG export terminals, there are ways for the PHMSA to ensure the community has access to information and a voice in safety management. In addition, PHMSA must make a version of their inspection reports available to the public, especially if there are code violations that put the community at risk. Some parishes or counties are supposed to have local emergency planning committees, but these have failed to be an effective mechanism for communicating with the public or producing adequate emergency plans.

Second, the PHMSA must enact a “reverse 911” system to alert impacted communities when there are leaks and explosions. Messages should provide residents with instructions on whether to evacuate or shelter in place, or to take other actions as needed.

Third, workers at LNG export terminals and associated infrastructure are often the first to know about problems, and can know about issues long before they manifest into leaks, vapor clouds, or explosions. Reporting issues, however, can be challenging and put workers at risk of retribution, including losing their job. The PHMSA must create an anonymous reporting hotline so that workers can anonymously and securely report issues that can be followed up with an inspection.

The government has an obligation to protect our communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. The PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure. I urge you to fulfill the PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.

"The ultimate test of a moral society is the kind of world that it leaves to its children."
-- Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Thank you for your consideration of my comments and for working to protect our health and safety. Please do NOT add my name to your mailing list. I will learn about future developments on this issue from other sources.

Sincerely,
Christopher Lish
San Rafael, CA

Title: Comment from Robyn  Thigpen
Comment: I’m writing in strong opposition to any deregulation of LNG safety standards under 49 CFR part 193. Louisiana communities, especially those living and working along our ship channels, are already overexposed to fire, explosion, and pollution risks from this industry. Foreign-flagged LNG tankers operating near narrow waterways and crowded ship channels already pose serious risks, espeically with the Coast Guard’s limited inspection authority. PHMSA’s updates to part 193 must not ignore these maritime hazards or the possibility that further weakening oversight could make them worse. These tankers operate near neighborhoods, workers, schools, and fishing camps. If anything goes wrong, the result could be catastrophic. We cannot afford to loosen standards when the existing ones are already inadequate. PHMSA must strengthen, not weaken, fire safety rules, enforceable inspections, and emergency response requirements to protect people, jobs, and the seafood industry that we’re already losing.

Title: Comment from Caroline Bauer
Comment: I urge PHMSA to reject any proposed changes to 49 CFR part 193 that prioritize industry cost savings over public health and environmental safety. The current modeling used to evaluate LNG facility risks is flawed—failing to account for still-air conditions, toxic releases, and cumulative damage to wetlands and coastal ecosystems. These facilities are loud, polluting, and surrounded by communities already burdened by industrial development. They’re also destroying our fisheries and the traditional seafood economy. PHMSA should reject the incorporation of NFPA 59A-2023 unless it includes enforceable protections for coastal communities, meaningful input from impacted residents, and safeguards against industry self-regulation. Louisianans deserve safe neighborhoods, clean air, and a future where our coastal communities can survive.

Title: Comment from David Singleton
Comment: Communities in Southwest Louisiana are already overburdened. Our region has already been devasted by a lack of regulations and faces an unfair risk to our safety and health. The risks multiply when so much hazardous infrastructure is packed into one region. Any expansion of LNG or other industrial activity, or any weakening of existing regulation, is inexcusable. PHMSA must use this rulemaking as an opportunity to strengthen oversight, not relax it. That means more transparent risk modeling, enforceable fire protection requirements, better coordination with maritime safety agencies, and full consideration of the impact to the enivironment. This region cannot handle more pollution, more risk, or more neglect. The health and safety of our people must come first.

Title: Comment from Eric Fournier
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Alex Cooperman
Comment:
I fully support the update of 49CFR193 by removing the references to the outdated 2001/2006 editions of NFPA 59A and replacing those with the references to the latest edition of NFPA59A. The references to the latest NFPA59A edition shall be updated throughout of the whole text of Part 193 document.

Title: Comment from Micah Six Eight Mission
Comment: This comment is about PHMSA-2019-0091-0012. I am not a scientist, I lead a community organization in Southwest Louisiana. As such, I attend the Local Emergency Planning Committee. At a recent meeting the first responders talked about their concerns that NONE of their departments were prepared or equipped to fight a fire from the water, which would be the only way to successfully fight a fire that resulted from an accident loading or unloading an LNG container. Overall, it sounded like none of them had any confidence they could successfully fight a fire on land, be it from a pipeline or in the facilities themselves. These facilities have come online so quickly with so little oversight it is frightening. While I can't respond in detail to the numbered questions in the proposed rules/regulations, I can say that the community of 500+ people that we work with and serve are very concerned about the way each segment of the approval process for these facilities is viewed and decided on as if they were independent of each other when it is very clear to us that they are not. In addressing safety concerns PHMSA should look at the entire picture, from ground to ship. Additionally, PHMSA should make sure that oversight of pipeline inside the facilities are part of the regulations. In closing, I saw many mentions of cost effectiveness in the document referenced here, obviously trying to curb costs for the operators. I saw no mention of the social, economic or environmental costs to the communities that surround these facilities and pipelines. THOSE COSTS SHOULD BE THE PRIMARY CONSIDERATION FOR ANY REGULATIONS/RULES.

Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091
With respect to the (ANPRM) solicitation of feedback, I am pleased to provide the following.  I am an engineer at an EPC with over twenty years of relevant experience in the siting, design, construction, and commissioning of LNG facilities regulated under the purview of various authorities and related standards both domestically and internationally.  
I applaud the effort to amend the Part 193 regulations for LNG facilities, alleviate unnecessary regulatory burdens, and harmonize codified requirements to bring regulation up to date with the best practices afforded by the NFPA 59A Technical Committee which is believed to be the most expedient, robust and enduring route to maintain LNG requirements.  The NFPA Technical Committee is comprised of industry experts, facility operators, and representatives from regulatory bodies including PHMSA, FERC, and USCG, all providing collective input on a continual cycle basis to ensure adoption of best practices for the safe design, construction, and operation of LNG facilities.
B.2
In relation of material differences in LNG facilities (size, complexity, etc.), there are risk differentiators in the scale and scope of a facility.  NFPA 59A (and Z276 as an example) recognizes this distinction and has undertaken efforts to define requirements based on the distinction.  In NFPA 59A, Chapter 17 addresses applicable requirements specific to Small Scale LNG Facilities meeting specific scale requirements; thus, small scale facilities should be required to comply with Chapter 17 of NFPA 59A, and large-scale facilities should require compliance with NFPA59A.
D.1
RE outdated requirements incorporated by reference in NFPA 59A-2001 and the impracticality applying those provisions in modern design, siting, and installation, there certainly exists material challenges to manage compliance with multiple editions of standards.  The challenges include confusion amongst stakeholders, achieving compliance with outdated codes, and validating equivalency between incorporated references and current practices.  For example, ASME Boiler Pressure Vessel Code, 1992 edition is referenced, however the design, testing, and delivery of an ASME BPV legally must be stamped and designed under the latest code edition in effect at the time of purchase.  Establishing equivalency between editions that are over three decades removed puts undue burden on contractor, owner, and supplier.  Similarly, another example is the ASME B 31.3 Process Piping standard which is referenced to the 1996 edition.  It is noted that each revision cycle of NFPA 59A includes a refresh of the referenced standards.  Further, the NFPA Technical Committee has cross-functional members who also serve on standards across the industry including as examples, ACI, API, ASME, and others.  This promotes a more robust understanding and maintenance of reference standards.
D.2
RE segregating the rulemaking process to updating references only to NFPA 59A 2023 edition, and forestalling a broader update to Part 193, it is my opinion that the opportunity to simplify and clarify the requirements of Part 193 in a broader sense will better serve all stakeholders by adopting the edition of NFPA 59A without at the time of the CFR amendment, and incorporation by reference in whole.  Part 193 can maintain exceptions that the body deems necessary, but this would be narrow and explicit, rather than the end user attempting to navigate multiple regulatory avenues of information (including FAQs).
D.4
In relation to extent of LNG operators’ general application of more recent additions of NFPA 59A, in general new facility builds utilize the latest NFPA 59A edition at the time of the facilities design inception (contract award) and only carve out explicit prior editions as required to comply with older versions of codes and standards if legally required.
D.5
RE broad incorporation by reference specific provisions by substituting NFPA 59A 2001 for NFPA 59A 2023, see response to question D.2.
E.2
RE to which edition of each standard should PHMSA update its part 193 regulations, please see response to D.2.  I recommend simplification of the part 193 regulations to incorporate by reference NFPA 59A latest edition at the time of the CFR adoption to permit the vast investment of Technical Committee and stakeholders time and resources in maintaining and evolving the NFPA 59A standard and associated references therein.
H.4
RE to how can PHMSA best design rulemaking to be deregulatory and lead to cost savings, I urge simplicity.  Industry mechanisms already exist to advance new technologies, adapt to a changing LNG landscape, address, and codify best practices and operating experience to advance the safety and operation of LNG facilities.  The ongoing work of the NFPA 59A Technical Committee which include designers, fabricators, engineers, operators, industry experts, and the arrayed regulatory bodies constitute that industry mechanism.

Title: Comment from Elliott Bales
Comment:
PHMSA-2019-0091-0012 Pipeline Safety: Amend... ,


Dear Secretary Duffy and Acting Administrator Kochman,

As a stakeholder interested in LNG infrastructure, I am deeply concerned about the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration's (PHMSA) upcoming update of LNG safety regulations.

These safeguards are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile methane gas and LNG infrastructure. It’s important that these are updated, as the existing guidelines are over 40 years old, are profoundly out of date, and don’t effectively create transparency and public safety. 

Rather than recognizing they urgently require updates to be effective, this process seeks to deregulate a critical agency in the interest of saving costs for the LNG industry rather than the people whose lives are on the line. I urge the Administration to prioritize safety, transparency, and accountability rather than industry profits. You should ensure workers and communities living, working, and recreating near pipeline infrastructure have effective standards to keep them safe.

In order to best improve their response, PHMSA should seek guidance from communities and workers that have experience with pipeline failures and explosions. In this process, PHMSA should be seeking stakeholder input on ways to set strong and specific standards for methane leakage reduction from methane gas pipeline infrastructure, avoid siting new gas pipeline infrastructure near existing sources of pollution, and the costs to the community of pipeline leakage, ruptures, explosion, and other failures. 

Thank you for this opportunity.

Title: Comment from Christian Smith
Comment:
I am writing in response to the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) to urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to strengthen safety rules for liquified methane gas (LNG) export terminals and reject any amendments that would undermine critical protections for workers and communities.

The current safeguards that are meant to protect workers and communities from dangerous and volatile LNG infrastructure are profoundly out of date and urgently require updates to be effective. We are deeply concerned by comments from administration officials claiming this process will be centered on deregulation and cost savings for industry, which would be a devastating step in the wrong direction. It is vital that PHMSA prioritizes transparency and public safety.

Along with the sharp expansion of U.S. LNG exports, we have seen a startling number of explosions, leaks, and other hazards at LNG facilities. The government has an obligation to protect communities from hazards by enforcing health and safety regulations for dangerous fossil fuel infrastructure. PHMSA must prioritize strong safety standards that center community input, worker safety, and transparency of the risks associated with living near LNG export infrastructure.

We urge you to fulfill PHMSA’s mandate to protect workers and communities by strengthening key safety rules for LNG export terminals.
